A child lies sleeping in calm repose,
AS sweet and fair as dewy rose;
Her little white hands are laid at rest
Over her gently heaving breast.
Sunny smiles on her red lips play.
Linger moment, then pass away
Forms and faces of earth and air
Fit through her mind as.she slumbers there
Amid the misty and mellow skies,
Their white wings dazzle her dreaming eyes
Until she wakens in mute dismay
While her fleeting fancies fade away.
She sleeps again-in her last repose;
She lies like withered and faded rose.
Over her forehead, pale and fair,
Ripple her tresseS of golden hair.
Her little white hands are laid at rest
Over her tranquil and lifeless breast.
Her voice is silent, and, come what may,
No smile will gladden. her lips of clay;
For the happy dreams she dreamed are


through;
How sweet to hope they all came true!

The oldest clergyman in America Mr. Boehm,

dist Episcopal church more impressive was
that the venerable preacher still retains his
faculties aud pronounced the benediction

seemed young to this senior of the Ameri-
can Republic. The scene reminds us

appearance Of ''Tamenund Of many days
in the council of his chiefs. 'They were all
aged" says the chronicler, ''but one in the
centre, who leaned upon his companions for

which the human race is seldom permitted to
attain. His frame, which had once been tall
and erect, like the cedar, was now bending
under the pressure of more than century"

the famous chief, as he recalled the vague
past, was felt by his children in the faith
for this Christian father who remembers the
birth Of the great Church which now extends
over continent, and can recall the time when
New York was but village and the popuous
country around it an almost unbroken forest.

No trumpet blast profaned
The day on which the Prince of Peace was born;


No bloody streamlet stained
Earths silver rivers on that sacred morn;


But Ger the peaceful plain
The war-horse drew the PEASANTS loaded vain.


The soldier had laid by
His sword and stripped the corset from his breast
And hung his helm on high,
The sparrow's Winter home and Summer nest


And with the same strong hand
That flung the barbed spear, he titled the land.


Oh time for which we yearn
Oh Sabbath of the nations, long foretoldl


Season of peace, returnl
Like late Summer when the year grows old;


When its sweet sunny days
Steep mead and mountain-side in golden haze.


For now two rival kings
Flaunt DER our bleeding land their hostile hags,


And every morning brings
The lowering vulture from the mountain crags


To where the battle plain
Is strewn with dead. the youth and flower Of Spain


Christ is not come while yet
Der half the earth the threat of battle lowers,


And our own fields are wet,
Beneath the battle-cloud, with crimson shower



Poured out where thousands die that one may reign


Yet soon DER half the earth,
In every temple, crowds shall kneel again


To celebrate His birth
Who brought the message of good will to men


And bursts of joyous song
Shall shake the roof above the PROSTATE throng.


Christ is not come while there
The men of blood whose crimes affront the skies,


Kneel down in act Of prayer,
Amid the Joyous strains. and when they RISE


Go forth, with sword and flame,
To waste the land in His mos. holy Name.


Oh when the day shall break
Der realms unlearned III warfares cruel arts,


And all their millions wake
To tasks of peaceful hands and loving hearts.


On such blessed morn
Well may the nations say that Christ is born


WILLIAM CULLEN BRYANT.

A story of sadness and superstition


comes to us from Indiana. In a lonely


spot on the hillside on small stream


known as Mad Lick, about two miles back


Of Dillsboro, stood log house, which, until


about six weeks ago, was occupied by a


man named Hutton (called Doe Hutton


and his family. One day while Hutton


was at work in the field, and and his wife
was engaged outside of the house, their
little girl, about three and half years old,
approached too near the open fireplace


and her clothing ignited. The mother was
not near enough to hear the child's screams


and when she entered the room the little
one was found burned to crisp and dead.


Near the fireplace the floor was scorched,
where child lay burning, and there was
also a mark on the wall of the room,
against which she had rnn in her agony.
She then ran to the bed, hid her head
under the clothes and there died. Her


body was terribly burned, but her head and
face were protected from the flames by the
bed clothing. Selling up the dead body Of
the child, the mother ran screaming with
it to where the father was at work. The
Huttons are believers in spiritual mani
festations, as are most Of the people in the
neighborhood. They have their regular
meetings, circles and also grips and pass
words for members of their association,


For several days after the death of the
child the Hutton family tried living in
the log cabin, but at length acknowledged
their inability to do SO, and moved into the
village of Dillsboro. They declared that
almost constantly they could hear cries for
help and screams of agony from the dead
child, mingled with weird music that rang
through the l:rnse. The neighbors also
said that they ,ould hear the shreks. The
horrifyiny sounds were kept up about the
homestead Of the Huttons until the neigh
bors at last declared they could no longer
bear them, and accordingly, few days
ago, in order to get rid of the suffering |
spirit, Hutton's house and barn were
burned to the ground.

risks were increased by reason Of the ten
ants using the building as basket factory,
then the whole policy and transfer was nul!
and void, if not, then the policy was good
and the plaintiffs bound to recover. A nice
point for the jury to settle. The whole
question farming on the point of increased
risk after the transfer of Insurance was
made from stock, &C., to the bull lding. ~

ers with the late improvements seem

and to insure getting machine farm
ers are giving their orders early, which
is very sensible thing. And judging

early won't be disappointed, while

want to use their machine can't all
get the Mccormick and will be obliged

favorites seem to be the two wheeled
combined Self Raker and Mower
"Advance. The Harvester that car
ries the two binders and the combined

cutter bars. This is very important.

are so well made that they don't snow
much wear where other machines

is strong argument in their favor,

machines at Dallas for the coming

one mile below the American Flat
scales. The up train for Carson, when
near the Baltic switch, q short dis
tance from Gold Hill, broke coup

the down grade, the hindmost loaded
with pig-iron., The brakemen jumped
off without injury, also the conductor.
The first part of the train dashed on to
Gold HILL They telegraphed to the
man at the scales to turn the switch
and run the cars off the track, knowing
a train was coming with which col
lisiOn was inevitable, unless the runa-
way cars were turned off the track.
For some reason the switch was not
turned and the collision occurred. The
coming train consisted of nine cars,
including one passenger car, and two
the former in advance. Clifford, the
engineer,of the Comstock, says the
loose cars came at speed of sixty
miles an hour. He shut off steam,
whistled down the brakes, and the
fireman, brakeman and engineer

iron car struck the ComsteclS, stove in
her boiler and swept. off her smoke
stack. She was wrecked. The shock
was heard at.Gold Hill, two miles dis
tant. The pig-iron car was knocked
into kindling wood. No lives were
lost, although the up train was con-

WASHINGTON Nov. 1S.-Some time ago serious ac-

pay-rolls of his department had been falsely made
out since 1872, 30 that workmen were charged on

eted by somebody having authority over the men,

received by Secretary Robson. The substance OF

tween Mr. Stratton and his chief clerk, and that the
accusations against the former were the result OF
this quarrel. The report, however, shows that MI

for period of year the frauds alleged had been
committed aud that the woIkmen had not been paid
the amount shown by the rolls 1t was not shown
that MIR. stratton was guilty of the fraud, but he

that the Board of Inquiry is not dissolved until the
responsibility is determined and the guilty persons
found.

Twas night,-all nature hushed. The song

slept. 1 dreamed. Methought, a youth


again,

plain;
'Mong sunny bowers, beside the ripping rll
That danced in glee adown the messy hill.
Fancied saw the old brown cot that stood
Close by the merry, music-haunted wood,
Where tangled vines and underbrush have


tried


Long years a little witching brook to hide,
And wandered through its halls a child again
And listened to the old familiar strain
My mother sang, while swinging swift the


reel


That gathered from the spindle of the wheel
Threads blue and white. And then stood


beside


My father, pleading for pick.a-pack ride
Just round the corner by the barley stack;
When, with a smile, he placed me on his back
And cantered off in all his manly mien,
While mother from the windows watched the


scene.


With rod and line coursed the limpid


stream.
Nor thought myself the subject of dream,
And noted how the tameless, timd trout r.
Alarmed at my advances, darted out
To seek some other peaceful, dark retreat,
Beyond the jar Of my intruding feet.
The brier-clad mound beside the streamlet,


where,
century old, has been preserved with care
The rough-hewn stone that marks the resting


place


Ofstranger settler, met my cautious pace.
The swallows flight, the drowsy hum of bees,
The soft wind whispering in the leafy trees,
The murmuring brook, the bridge the water


fall,


And youth and home; I so enjoyed them all.
At last spied the elm above the spring,
And in its branches hung the same old swing
Iprized so much in youth-in days gone by;
And with happy. wild, exultant cry,
leaped upon the board to ride again,
Like bird upon the air; my giddy brain
Had lost its nerve; fell. and with scream
Awoke to find twas but an idle dream;
Alas, to find twas only but dream.

The Jonesville town lot speculation

MORNING.
The morn was gently breaking,
With q sky serene and clear.
Full many heart was quaking
With the agony of fear.
The polls were opened early,
And the voting slow began,
With sour looks and surly,
The boys commenced to plan.
The Independents came prepared,
To wage desperate fight.
They vowed to all they were not scared,
For they were men of might.
They charged upon the polls in force,
AS Greeks weuld charge a wall,
With men convened from every source,
They saw their victims fall.
Along their ranks you heard them prate
AS Fastening to the fray,
"These fares and freights and water rates
We swear we'll never pay.'


EVENING.
The breeze was gently starting,
And the sun was sinking low,
Sworn friends were sadly parting
With footsteps tired and slow.
There were many anxious faces,
There were many throbbing hearts,
Standing firmly at their places
Where they'd nobly done their paIts.
The contest was firm one.
Hot waged on every side,
By many an Independent son,
Who tried to stem the tide,
Begrimed their tired workers,
Saw all their strong-holds fall.
They drove the sulky lurkers,
AS cattle from the stall.
But the cause of Truth was mighty,
All their efforts were in vain,
The hopes they nursed were flighty,
And only gave them pain.
In solid ranks, the voters
Came up unto the polls,
Democracy promoters,
They voted for their souls.
AS the storm king sweeps the ocean.
As truth does crush lie,
We crushe d in wild commotion,
This Independent cry.
AS the leaves are swept in Autumn,
BY the fierce winds angry call,
We captured and we caught 'em,
Our congressman and all.

arms, legs and trunk were moved
with writings and contortions, as
though the form had life and sense OF
feeling. The Indian had died in a
drunken debauch, and when the flames
penetrated to his entrails the alcohol
ignited and burned in blue flame
over the body for several minutes.
Chief Francisco, who was boss stoker,
then replenished the fire, and with a
long stick pushed the projecting limbs
into the center of the flames, uttering
grunts of satisfaction at the successful
progress of the cremation. The whole
operation required about three hours
time, although not much was to be
seen of the body after the first hour.
When the burning was over the re-
manning ashes were buried and the
Indians solemnly filed away, mutter-
ing, in their tongue, the equivalent to
"Peace to his ashes.n

intendent Ellis has not yet explained why
he suffered the Third Avenue Savings Bank
to continue to impose upon the public and
to obtain deposits on false pretences after
his examination of the affairs of the bank

hopelessly bankrupt An explanation from

acts. The meeting of the depositors may

how far the officers and stockholders of q

LONDON, August 11th.-An Italian
letter states that no proclamation of
unity, no unification of political and
administrative legislation, can destroy
the traditional fact of seven States,
with seven different capitals and local
interests, and that at the present mo-
ment Italy has resolved herself into
her component parts. The news Of
the triumph of the Clerical party in
Venice, Florence, Genoa and Verona
have raised the hopes of that party.
Almost the only topic which interests
all Italy at present is precisely these
municipal elections in Venice. The
Liberals allied themselves with the
Clerical party against the Moderates
and succeeded, but in Florence and
Genoa, especially the latter city, the
Moderates allied themselves against
the Liberals and the Clerical party
obtained a still more brilliant success;
for out of 1850 votes, 3,4S2 went to the
Urn, and out of sixty-one Councillors
elected, thirty-seven were Clerical,
and but twenty-three Liberals sue
ceeded. The entire population are
anxiously awaiting news from the
Neapolitan election, although the re-
suit is certain. The Claricals will
carry the day, and for the first time
since the annexation of 1860 the Mod
crates and Clericals have openly and
avowedly joined hands and formed an
offensive and defensive alliance
against the Liberals, who have here
tofore administered the province. An
explanation of this change is that
nearly all the Communes in Italy are
over head and ears in debt. The peo-
pie who clamored for fetes and mOnu-
ments, public gardens and boulevards,
now that the bill is presented, are
appalled, at the sum total, and, blam-
ing their Mayor and Council, looked
around them for new men, and could

Our yachtsmen were unlucky yesterday
in sailing the "Kane" regatta The weather
was inconstant and played sad tricks with
the vessels. OF the sixteen yachts that
proudly unfurled their sails there were only
eight which went out into the sea- Commo-
dore Kingsland's pretty vessel, the Alarm
went ashore on the West Bank, but received
no special harm. The Mohawk, Vice Commo-
dore Gamers celebrated yacht, was becalmed
tune befell the Resolute. Outside there was
heavy head sea, which carried away the
masts of the Peerless. These misfortunes,
small and great, made the day one of inter-
est if not of enjoyment We can hardly call
it regatta where one-half of the vessels
fail to take part from causes beyond their
control. AS the turfmen would say, it was q
'dead heat" and we should have another
meeting, if for no other purpose than to show
what our yachtsmen can do with an autumn
breeze and an autumn sea. The only first
class schooner that went over the course was
the Atalanta. There were two second class
schooners- Comet and the Estelle-the
former winning. None Of the first class
sloops sailed the course, while the
Sadie was the only second class
sloop that was fortunate enough to
do SO. We regret that Rear Commodore
Kane, who gave the prizes for this regatta
was not more fortunate, as his generous and
enterprising liberality, and his zeal for the
interests of the cluh deserved all the hon0rs
that can rest upon yachtsman's flag. Our
yachting clubs were never in a more prosper
Gus condition, and especially the New York
Club, under the command of Commodore
Kingsland The New York Club has
now fine club house at the anchorage
on Staten Island. This is like the club
house at Cowes, the rendezvous Of the Eng
lish squadrons, and it is owing largely to
Vice Commodore Garner, whose efforts on
behalf Of yachting deserve special recognition
and honor

In busy street of London there

Wondering away with age. OF course
it has history. Many years ago, u
certain nobleman was engaged to be

ding morning arrived, the breakfast

some room. the bridegroom was ready

forming him that she had eloped that
morning with his best man, n gay cap
tain of dragons. The disappointed
bridegroom quietly went alone to the
room in which the wedding breakfast

up the shutters and drew the blinds,
locked the door and took the key. He
gave orders that the door should be
nailed up and barred with padlocked
bar, aud no one should enter the room
again. When the house was let, 1t
was stipulated that the room in ques-
ton should remain untouched. The
nobleman died some years afterward,
but the room has never been entered
since he closed it, aud there are the
"wedding meats" Wondering silently
away, and the ornaments crumbling
into dust in the funeral gloom.

Over the landscape far and near

sweets


In memoriam of the summer days.
Grandfather thinks of the years gone by,
The spring-time first of his merry youth,
And then the summer of manhood's joys,
When his heart grew warm with love and


truth.


"Alas!' he murmurs. "that time has assed,

Kisses the spot where loving hands
Laid him down when his life was done.
And over the meadow, over the hills,
The breeze goes sobbing the livelong day
For the fair sweet summer whose life went


out
With the shadow of winter chill and gray.

A TRAMP KILLED BY WoMAN.-A dispatch
dated Mlansport, Pa, Aug. 22d, says "Mrs.
Morgan Calvert, young widow, who lives with
her brother two miles from this place, was left
alone in her isolated house for several days
last week. On Thursday afternoon a rough fell


low called at the house, and, after asking Mrs.
Calvert many questions, begged for a supper
and nights lodging. He was refused. There
upon he went away, muttering to himself
little later Mrs Calvert was obliged to 60 out,
and on her return she saw man crouching
behind the door between the sitting room and
her bedroom. He did not seem to see her, and
she saw him only through narrow crack
There were firearms in the house, and Mrs. Cal
vert knew how to use them. Without an out.
cry, she went up stairs and got revolver, and
hiding it under her apron, started boldly for
the room in which the tramp was lurking.
As Mrs. Calvert approached the door, the
man threw it open suddenly, jumped out, and
struck her in the face. Recovering quickly
from the blow, she drew her pistol, upon seeing
which the tramp turned to flee. She fired once
and wounded him, and then started to pursue
him. As be disappeared around the house she
fired again, at which he turned about and cried,
"Don't shoot again, woman. | am dead man,
now" AS he spoke he staggered against
fence, and then fell. He begged for aid, and
Mrs. Calvert arranged him in comfortable
position, after which she started for physi


clan. As she approached the house, the tramp
who had first called upon her rushed out and
escaped and under the great excitement she
fell fainting near the roadside. Two hours la
ter she was discovered by friends, who listened
to her story and went to find the man whom
she had wounded. He was lying dead"

NEW YORK DRY GOODS MARKET.-Cotton
goods present the same remarkable steadi-
ness in value which has been their charac-
teristic for many weeks past. There were
very few price fluctuations during the week,
but few popular brands of brown and

the agents, and the general line was excep-
tiOnally firm. There was fair package de-

sheetings, which continue closely sold up to

tiles OF acknowledged reputation found ready

side makes experienced some trouble in

fabrics.-N. Y. Bulletin, 24th

| Two lions, two leopards, and tame
black panther have for some months
been kept i'll one cage in Barnum's
hippodrome. The lions are separated
from their companions through the
night by iron bars, but in the day
| time the bars are Withdrawn, and the
animals form sshappy family"
| No sooner were the bars taken out
yesterday morning than the leopard
made a spring for the panther's throat.
The panther was young, but his mus
cles were like iron and his skin as
thick as sole-leather, and he struck
the leopard a blow with one of his
fore-paws that laid him sprawling on
the floor of the cage. In an instant
the leopard was on his feet again, and
the animals stood face to face. For
fully minute they glared and growl-
ed, and then, with a shock that nearly
turned the cage on'the side, they met
again, each trying to grasp the other
by the throat.


The employees of the hippodrdme,
attracted by the noise of the conflict,
tried, with iron bars and spears, to
separate the combatants, but without
avail. Seasoned spears were snapped
into like straws, and even the keeper
of the animals dared not approach the
cage.


The leopard, with an unexpected
spring, fixed himself on the panther's
back, and, taking the loose skin on
the back Of the latter's neck between
his teeth, gave the panther toss
against the side of the cage that bent
the thick iron bars nearly double. For
a minute there was great danger that
all the beasts in the cage would es-
cape. The top of the cage was broken
and the floor was split. But the bat
tie was over, for the panther, without
sound, struck the floor of the cage
lifeless.


But the leopard was not satisfied
with the death of his antagonist. No
sooner was he convinced that he
could approach with safety than, seiz-
ing the panther's head between his
fore paws, he gave him tearing with
the sharp claws of his hind feet that
nearly stripped the skin from his
body. Then he began with his teeth,
and before the employees could inter-
fere nearly half of the dead panther
had been eaten by the leopard.


When at length sufficient force
lad been collected around the cage,
the keeper who had tanned the panther
entered the den. There upon the floor
lay his pets silky black skin, almost
entire. His body, not yet cold, quiv-
cred and his eyes glared. The leopard
crouched in corner of the cage, sat
isfied with his meal. The iron bars
were soon replaced, and the leopard
was prevented from doing further
mischief.


At the afternoon performance the
leopard was SO unruly that it was
deemed unsafe for the trainer to enter
the cage; but the bars were kept in
their places and no more damage was
done.

SACRAMENTO, February 10Th. To
day was appointed for the execution
of Estrada and Gotta. A great crowd
gathered around the Court House all
day, hoping to be able to see the exc
cution, but the Sheriff enforced the
rule to have the execution as private
as possible. The relatives of the two
men have been with them all day.
Many persons were gathered on the
neighboring house-tops to see the exc
cution. The men breakfasted about
half-past 10 this morning. AT o'clock
this afternoon about 250 persons were
admitted, and shortly after the prison.
ers, supported by officers and preceded
by the priests, mounted the scaffold.
Gotta looked pale, but not muscle
quivered. Estrada was weak, though
firm. After prayer by the priest the
black caps were drawn over their faces,
the ropes were adjusted and the drop
fell. Estrada struggled violently some
time, and Gotta a little. Estrada's
body will be taken to San Francisco
for burial, and Gotta will be buried
here. Estrada's mother and sister
were both under the influence of chlo-
roform, and their lives are despaired
of. Mrs. Gotta took leave of the boys
at noon, giving both her blessing.

MAHoNEY City, Pa, June 3d.-At 3
o'clock to-day, Sheriff Warner tele-
graphed that his posse had been fired
upon, and asked for military assist
ance. The Pottsville Light Infantry
and Gowanus Guards Immediately
left by special train for this place. On
their arrival they found that the mob
had skunk away to the outskirts of the
town. The citizens are greatly ex-
cited. All places of business are closed,
The first disturbance occurred at Tyler
& Co.'s colliery, when Sheriff Agnew
and his posse ordered the rioters to
disperse. One of their chiefs fired
upon the Sheriff. The firing then be-
came general, the rioters firing VOL
ley on the citizens, who were outnum-
bered. Henry Lieutenberger, police
man, was wounded and is in a critical
condition. Henry Lockman was
wounded in the leg; VIM. Encke was
shot in the head and another man in
the shoulder. Eight rioters were
wounded and carried away, and one
killed. The strikers have dispersed in
different directions.


Col. Huntzeinger has established his
headquarters in the Mansion House,
and his troops are quartered in the
City Hall. Much excitement exists.
The miners will again resume work to-
morrow.

The position of sufferance which Turkey
holds in Europe is significantly demonstrated
in the action of the three Imperial Powers
Germany, Austria and Russia-on the Herze-
govina insurrection. They appear to have
united in proposal which will settle for the
present the difficulty with which the
Porte is contending This proposal
demands that Turkey shall grant certain
reforms and give certain guarantees to carry
them out There is scarcely shadow of
doubt that Turkey will accept the condi-
tions without giving herself very much con-
Germ whether she can fulfil them. She will
submit to them nominally, because she
must. Her weakness and isolation forbid
any other course but, with Oriental
cunning, she knows that her very
weakness will 60 a long way to protect
her from anything more hurtful thana diplo-
matte humiliation. She knows that she
would not be mouthful apiece for the three
Powers who are settling her insurrection for
her, but she is also aware that there would
be small likelihood of peaceful agreement
between them over the extent of each bite.
Indeed, she will see that her conclusions are
justified by the delicate manner in which
the three Powers have approached the
present little difficulty. Neither Germany
nor Russia could trust the other with the
drafting of proposal touching Turkish in
terests, and hence Austria, which could
always be held in check by the other two,
has been allowed to frame it. In the discus
sion between Bismarck and Gortschakoff at
Berlin the condition of the insurgent rayahs
held small part beside the more absorbing
question as to what may happen to the Otto
man Empire when the day of makeshift COM
promise and empty guarantee has gone by.
England is steadily preparing to take her
portion in the land of the Pharaohs, and
Gortschakoff is probably pondering how the
old Muscovite dream of a Russian flag over
Stamboul may become a reality.

The recent wave of polar cold which swept
over the country from west to east has made
no ordinary impress upon the meteorology of
the month. Its central course seems to have
been more directly through the interior, in
ficting severe temperatures upon Tennessee
and the Southern States, and enabling the
Frost King once more to set his wintry seal
on the watercourses that find their way to the
Atlantic. Preceding this frigid spell there
were heavy and extensive rains in the interior
basin of the Mississippi, which will 60 far
toward restoring the balance of moisture which
has been lost ever since last July.


But scarcely had this severe frost and it's &C.
companying conditions moved off the coast
when the weather reports of Saturday an
nounced another rapid and unusually high
barometric rise in the extreme Northwest
Bitter experience has taught us in the Eastern
States that these high barometers of the
Northwest portend approaching cold, and are
the timely signals for us to arm ourselves
against the polar blast. These two cold waves
following each other in quick succession will
chill the Continent and prepare it to act as q
good condenser when the subsequent vapor-
laden winds of the spring begin to blow from
the Gulf and the sea. The qualification of
the rivers and small streams will relieve the
pressure on the Ohio and it's lower tributaries
now in flood. But the water thus held tenn
porarily will, as spring advances, be dis
tributed with greater benefit to agriculture
Meantime we may look out for the cold, and
hope that with it will pass the crisis of the
winter

and farmers that what is needed is ''more
money" an imitation of the currency, more

do not tell them how ''more money" of this

plain words, they are committing fraud

together could not get out single cent
''more money" could not initiate the cur

Connecticut will hold her State elec-

opened lively and has grown warmer

ance party aggregates about five
